subject: Banking
title: Redlining: Lending Discrimination
description: Learn Redlining: Lending Discrimination in one minute.

hook.text: US banks drew red lines on maps around Black neighborhoods. Inside those lines, no loans were approved for decades.

buildup.text: Starting in the 1930s, the FHA rated neighborhoods by 'risk.' Minority areas were labeled hazardous and denied.

discovery.text: Without loans, neighborhoods couldn't develop. Property values stayed low. The wealth gap widened for generations.

twist.text: Redlining was outlawed in 1968. But its effects persist.

climax.text: Redlining shows how lending decisions shape entire communities. Denied credit means denied opportunity for generations.

punchline.text: Banned in 1968. The wealth gap from redlining still exists today.

quiz.question: What was redlining?
options: Denying loans to neighborhoods based on racial composition

details.summary: Redlining was the systematic denial of financial services to residents of predominantly Black neighborhoods, where banks literally drew red lines on maps around areas deemed too risky to lend in, regardless of individual creditworthiness.
details.whyItMatters: Redlining created wealth gaps that persist generations later. Communities denied mortgages could not build home equity, the primary wealth-building vehicle for middle-class Americans, creating racial wealth disparities that endure today.
takeaways: Banks and the government systematically denied loans to Black neighborhoods
The Fair Housing Act of 1968 outlawed redlining but its effects persist
Formerly redlined neighborhoods remain poorer than surrounding areas today

faq.question: How did redlining work?
faq.answer: The Home Owners' Loan Corporation created maps color-coding neighborhoods. Green meant safe for lending, red meant hazardous. Red areas were overwhelmingly minority neighborhoods. Banks used these maps to deny mortgages regardless of individual qualifications.

faq.question: Does lending discrimination still exist?
faq.answer: Formal redlining is illegal, but studies consistently show that Black and Hispanic applicants are denied mortgages at higher rates even with similar credit profiles. Algorithmic lending has introduced new forms of potential discrimination through proxy variables.
